entry.title: Task success is not harness evidence: what Trial by Trace measures
entry.summary: A benchmark of 3,420 agent runs scores the task outcome and the harness's own obligations separately. In 31.1% of runs the task passed while at least one harness criterion failed.
entry.content:
A new benchmark of AI agent harnesses reports that a passed task does not, by itself, show that the harness met its own obligations. Across 3,420 runs (4 harnesses, 9 models, 95 tasks), the authors find that 31.1% of runs met every task criterion while failing at least one harness criterion, and that ranking harnesses by task success gives a different order than ranking them by harness criteria. Every number below is the authors'. We ran, reproduced and measured nothing.

What the study holds fixed and what it varies

The object under test is the native harness: the software that builds the model's context, exposes tools, carries calls and results, keeps state and enforces permissions. The model, task, environment and budgets are controlled inputs; the evaluator and capture machinery are treated as measurement apparatus, so apparatus failures are not counted as harness defects. The harnesses are Claude Code, Codex, DeepSeek Harness and OpenClaw. Each runs the same 95 tasks with each of 9 model groups, giving 855 matched model and task cells per harness. Tasks cover seven reliability components (context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, verification). Each task carries two score sheets: an Agent layer (required actions, deliverables, checked against authoritative state) and a Harness layer (whether the native system delivered information and executed faithfully).

Source: Zhiyong Cao, Hengjie Zhu, Yongxin Wang, Xuchen Li, Jintao Li, Shuxia Liu, Dunqiang Liu, Bo Wang, Kairan Zhang, Cong Lin, JiangDi Yu, Siyuan Liu, Sijia Yao, Yi-Liang Wei, Lingxu Ma, Aijia Wang, Anxin Chen, Zixian Wei, Xiang Ruan, Ruizhi Xu, Ruqian Shi, Baihua Xiao and Sicheng Zhou (TraceLite AI; names in section 9), "Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution", arXiv:2610.32285v1, Abstract, sections 2.2, 3.1, 3.2.3, 4.1, 4.3, arxiv.org/abs/2610.32285v1.

Two layers, two rankings

A run counts as task success only if no Agent criterion scored zero. Over all 3,420 runs, 1,351 (39.5%) met that bar, and only 286 (8.4%) passed every criterion in both layers. The 31.1% figure (1,065 runs; abstract, sections 1, 5.5 and 8, Table 10) counts runs with task success and at least one failed Harness criterion, over the same 3,420 runs.

The rankings split. Claude Code had the highest Agent task success (44.0% of its 855 runs); OpenClaw had the highest Harness macro rate (72.0%, the mean of each run's share of passed Harness criteria). Harness macro rates spanned 12.2 points, from Codex at 59.8% to OpenClaw at 72.0%; task success spanned 8.2 points, from Codex at 35.8% to Claude Code at 44.0%.

Who decided: criteria with a task oracle were scored by deterministic verifiers; semantic criteria were scored by one fixed LLM Judge (deepseek-v4-flash), whose output limit was 4,096 tokens in 1,966 evaluations, 8,192 in 1,452 and 32,000 in two.

Source: the same work, Abstract, sections 1, 4.2, 4.3, 5.1, 5.2, 5.5, 8, Tables 6 and 10, arxiv.org/abs/2610.32285v1.

Which record speaks for what

Evidence authority is specific to the question. Environment or simulator state establishes what happened. Changed artifacts establish the persisted deliverable. The native model-facing record establishes what the model could see. An agent's final messages establish only what the agent asserted. Execution probes owned by the runner record process outcome, timeout and approvals "independent of prose reports".

A tool action can exist in several non-equivalent forms: the apparatus may know a process timed out while the model-facing result omits it, and keeping both is what makes a fidelity criterion possible. Tasks deliberately include nonzero exits paired with success-shaped artifacts. The runner's own result file supplies identity, but its score field is not the final-score authority. The paper does not, however, report a measured rate at which harness or agent claims of completion disagree with end state; only 1 of the 95 tasks sits in the Verification component, defined as consistency of completion claims with authoritative outcomes.

Source: the same work, sections 2.3, 3.1, 3.2.2, 3.3.1, 3.3.2, Table 3, Figure 4, section 4.2, arxiv.org/abs/2610.32285v1.

What a zero and a link do not prove

Attribution here is between the Harness layer and the Agent layer, not between harness and model. A Harness zero means the criterion was violated or the selected evidence did not establish it; an empty evidence selection also scores zero. A criterion marked "not exercised" is resolved from the Agent outcome, so the two layers are not statistically independent. Results use the raw zero sets, without the bypass adjustment the method defines.

A failure link is activated when a predeclared Harness criterion and Agent criterion both fail and the declared condition matches. The authors state this is a candidate, not causal propagation: validation requires manual review of event order, an observed intermediate distortion and competing explanations. The labels "harness_caused" and "agent_caused" are operational. The paper reports candidate links in 842 of 1,700 runs failing both layers (49.5%) and no count of validated links.

Source: the same work, sections 2.3, 3.4, 3.5, Tables 4 and 5, sections 4.3 and 5.5, Table 10, arxiv.org/abs/2610.32285v1.

Limits stated by the authors

Each cell holds one selected execution, including replacement runs from earlier recovery, so the authors do not estimate repeatability within a cell. They state that task revisions and recovery runs limit causal reading of differences between harnesses, and that they do not estimate selector recall, Judge agreement or candidate link precision. We checked the full arXiv PDF of v1, including tables and appendices. The authors add that coverage across mechanisms is uneven (section 6.1).

Source: the same work, sections 3.6, 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 6.1, arxiv.org/abs/2610.32285v1.

What we proposed, and why we wait

Our research desk read the paper and proposed a trial: score the outcome a harness reports separately from the measured end state. This is inspired by the paper's split of evidence authority, not a copy of its two layers. Status: proposed, with no owner decision; nothing has been run. The arXiv listing gives CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for the paper text. The paper links a code repository (github.com/TraceLite-AI/TraceTrial-Bench) but states no code licence, so reuse of the authors' code is on hold pending a licence check.

Source: the same work, arXiv listing, title page and section 4.4, arxiv.org/abs/2610.32285v1.

entry.title: Agent-written verifiers in VerifierBench rejected invalid solutions more reliably than they accepted valid ones
entry.summary: A new benchmark asks agents to write executable verifiers for 222 tasks and scores them on 4,993 hidden test cases. Across 19 models in one common harness, task-averaged acceptance of valid solutions ranged from 21.1% to 70.2%, while rejection of invalid ones ranged from 79.2% to 96.3%; in the records analysed for nine models, verifiers that rejected every case of their task produced 87.9% to 96.0% of false rejections.
entry.content:
In VerifierBench, executable verifiers written by agents were better at rejecting invalid solutions than at accepting valid ones. Scored against reference labels on hidden test cases, across 19 models run in one common harness, the task-averaged rate at which generated verifiers accepted valid solutions ranged from 21.1% to 70.2%, while the rate at which they rejected invalid solutions ranged from 79.2% to 96.3%. Every model accepted less reliably than it rejected. In the records analysed for nine models, verifiers that returned FAIL on every test case of their task produced 87.9% to 96.0% of each model's false rejections.

These findings are about generated verifiers' verdicts on hidden test cases. The numbers are the authors'; we have not run or reproduced anything.

What the benchmark holds fixed and what it varies

The object under test is a generated verifier: a program an agent writes from the same instruction and environment a solver would receive, which must return PASS or FAIL for any candidate solution. A finding here is about that program's verdict on a candidate, not about whether the task itself was solved.

The authors hold the tasks, the hidden test cases and the reference labels fixed. They vary the model and the harness, the agent framework that runs it. The main comparison runs 19 models in one harness; 17 further configurations bring the total to 36.

VerifierBench has 222 tasks from six open-source agent benchmarks, covering tool-call, state and code tasks, with 4,993 hidden test cases. Of these, 1,566 are labelled PASS: 222 reference solutions and 1,344 valid variants that change presentation, implementation or execution path. The other 3,427 are labelled FAIL: 2,629 ordinary errors and 798 attacks on verification.

Source: Jianing Yin, Ziyi Chen, Hao Wang, Yiyou Sun, Zijian Jin, Dawn Song, Daoan Zhang, "VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents", arXiv:2610.28679v1, 19 October 2026, sections 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1 and Table 1, arxiv.org/abs/2610.28679v1.

Who decides what is correct

Each test case gets a construction label before any verifier runs. The authors then screen labels and the benchmarks' own source verifiers with a six-check audit they call Verifier4Verifier: replay, repeatability, provenance, input-label consistency, trivial baselines and mutation testing. Its trivial-baseline check requires the suite to expose verifiers that always accept, always reject or accept only the reference solution.

The audit started from 267 tasks and excluded 45 with confirmed source defects. On the 222 retained tasks, replay agreed on every test case, so each construction label equals the reference verifier's decision. Generated verifiers are scored against that reference label. The authors note that this agreement does not certify that every label is semantically correct.

Source: the same work, section 2.3, Appendix B and Limitations, arxiv.org/abs/2610.28679v1.

How acceptance and rejection are counted

The true positive rate is the share of positive cases that receive PASS, and the true negative rate the share of negative cases that receive FAIL, each computed per task and averaged across tasks. A timeout, crash, missing verifier or malformed output gives no valid decision and stays in the denominator without credit.

The primary score, normalized balanced accuracy, is true positive rate plus true negative rate minus 100, so a verifier that always says FAIL scores 0. Across the 19 models in the common harness it ranged from 10.6 to 62.1.

The gap is mostly active rejection, not silence. Counted over test cases rather than averaged by task, explicit FAIL accounted for 57.1% to 100% of each model's unaccepted positive cases. The authors state that rankings are point estimates without repeated generations or significance tests.

Source: the same work, sections 2.4 and 3.2, Table 2, Appendix G and Limitations, arxiv.org/abs/2610.28679v1.

Where the false rejections sit

The authors call a verifier all-reject if it returns a valid FAIL on every test case of its task.

The 87.9% to 96.0% figure is the share of each model's false rejections (FAIL on cases the reference label marks PASS) that came from all-reject verifiers. It is computed on an archived export of per-task records for nine of the 19 models, not on final per-task records for all of them. A separate batch for one model under four conditions shows the same pattern: 68 to 75 of the 222 verifiers were all-reject and produced 93.3% to 95.5% of false rejections.

A low rate of accepted attacks did not mean the verifier was good. On state tasks, one model in the common harness accepted 0.0% of attack cases but only 23.0% of positive cases.

Source: the same work, sections 3.2 and 3.4, Appendix F and Appendix H, arxiv.org/abs/2610.28679v1.

Why self-tests missed it in the inspected cases

Table 4 lists 16 verifiers from 12 tasks, all from one model's trace batch under four conditions, whose rejections the authors attribute after reading code and generation traces. They were selected to explain observed failures, so this shows mechanisms, not prevalence. The attributed checks are ones the task does not require, such as a tool allowlist that omits a permitted read-only query or a keyword list that omits one of the task's items.

For eight of these verifiers, the agent's self-tests used only solutions the faulty check already allowed. For the other eight, no positive self-test ever returned a complete PASS during generation; at evaluation those eight rejected all 72 of their positive judgments.

Source: the same work, sections 4.1 to 4.3 and Table 4, arxiv.org/abs/2610.28679v1.

What we are doing with it

On 18 November our research desk read this paper and proposed a bounded trial: 12 to 20 synthetic frozen agent traces with independent ground truth, legitimate alternative paths, invalid mutations, and deliberate deny-all and accept-all sentinels. It would compare an existing verifier against a gate balanced on positive and negative cases, at fixed budget and identical evidence, and report true and false positives, true and false negatives and abstentions separately. The proposed rejection rule: any forbidden action accepted, or valid-variant acceptance below a predeclared baseline.

The status is proposed. There is no owner decision, and nothing was run or reproduced. The lesson we take is that a verifier which rejects everything looks safe on negative-only tests, so positive cases and an explicit UNKNOWN are needed.

This continues yesterday's item on whether verifier judgments survive abstraction of agent evidence (contract.place/en/journal/verification-transport-2026-11-18); we are not opening a separate initiative.

Source: the same work, section 2.4, for the metric definitions the trial would reuse; the trial itself is our proposal, arxiv.org/abs/2610.28679v1.

entry.title: Correct verifier verdicts failed in 20.3% to 31.0% of cases once agent evidence was abstracted
entry.summary: A new study holds agent traces fixed and changes only what an LLM verifier can see. Among judgments that were correct on the full trace, 31.0% failed under macro abstraction and 20.3% under history compaction; overall, restoring the execution provenance recovered 85.5% of failures across all three abstraction boundaries.
entry.content:
When an LLM verifier judges an agent trace correctly and the same trace is then shown to it through a compacted history, a delegation boundary or a macro action, in views the authors constructed from frozen traces, the correct judgment does not always survive. Sheshanarayana and Goli held the trace, the ground truth, the criterion and the verifier fixed and changed only the view. Among judgments that were correct on the native view, 31.0% failed under macro abstraction, 30.9% under delegation and 20.3% under history compaction. Putting the original provenance back recovered 85.5% of those failures.

What was measured

The authors call the property Verification Transport: a verifier judgment that is correct on the native execution view should stay correct when the same execution is exposed through an abstraction. They built matched native, abstracted and restored views of frozen trajectories from four benchmarks: 250 trajectories from AgentProcessBench, 758 from ATBench, 441 pairwise comparisons from PlanRewardBench and 754 trajectories from AgentDojo. These counts are the instances that met each benchmark's eligibility rules for matched construction.

Three boundaries were tested. Macro abstraction hides low-level operations behind a higher-level action. Delegation hides a sub-execution behind an agent boundary and shows only the call and its result. Compaction replaces an earlier region of history with a marker. Seven verifier backbones ran under four protocols: direct judgment, evidence-grounded judgment, provenance-seeking agentic judgment, and a deliberative audit of the evidence-grounded verdict. All verifiers ran at temperature 0.

Source: Disha Sheshanarayana, Sai Linisha Reddy Goli, "Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation", arXiv:2611.18471v1, 13 November 2026, arxiv.org/abs/2611.18471v1.

How the failure rate is counted

The Verification Transport Failure Rate (VTFR) is conditional. Its population is only the instances the verifier judged correctly on the native view. Correctness is judged by comparing the verifier's verdict with the benchmark's ground-truth label; the verifier is the LLM under test. Within that population, VTFR counts every instance whose abstracted verdict is either wrong or not usable. Abstentions, unresolved outputs and protocol-invalid responses count as failures.

Pooled rates sum numerators and denominators across cells instead of averaging percentages. The 31.0%, 30.9% and 20.3% figures pool all four benchmarks, seven models and four protocols. The authors state that VTFR measures the stability of initially correct judgments, not overall verifier accuracy. Across benchmarks, aggregate VTFR ranged from 25.5% to 32.2% under macro abstraction, from 26.1% to 32.9% under delegation and from 16.2% to 24.7% under compaction.

Source: the same work, sections 4.2 and 5.1 and Appendix C (including C.1), arxiv.org/abs/2611.18471v1.

Two ways to fail

The paper splits VTFR into Wrong Verdict and No Verdict, both over the same native-correct denominator, and the two sum to VTFR. Under macro abstraction, the overall split was 13.4% wrong and 17.7% no verdict. Under delegation it was 13.2% and 17.7%; under compaction, 12.2% and 8.0%.

Protocols differed sharply. Direct judgment had the lowest pooled VTFR, 16.4% under macro abstraction, but its failures were almost all wrong verdicts: 15.8% wrong and 0.7% no verdict. The deliberative audit had the highest, 49.3%, made up of 9.4% wrong and 39.9% no verdict. The authors warn that a lower failure rate does not necessarily mean a more reliable verifier, and that, because VTFR is conditioned on native-correct judgments, which may be different instance subsets for different protocols, protocol comparisons are not paired on identical instances and should account for those differences.

Source: the same work, section 5.1, Appendix E.1, Table 4, and Appendix E.2, arxiv.org/abs/2611.18471v1.

What restoring provenance recovered

Each abstracted view has a restoration condition that reintroduces the original operations, the delegated trajectory or the original history from the same frozen trace. The Restoration Recovery Rate (RRR) counts, among native-correct instances that failed after abstraction, the share that became correct and usable again. The Restoration Degradation Rate (RDR) counts, among instances that stayed correct after abstraction, the share whose verdict became wrong or unusable after restoration.

Pooled over everything, restoration recovered 85.5% of failures and degraded 5.2% of preserved judgments. Recovery was 87.9% for macro abstraction, 86.9% for delegation and 79.8% for compaction. In an ablation on two benchmarks with two models, a plain re-query recovered 22.5% to 33.1%, a lossy restoration of action and tool identities 34.0% to 53.9%, and exact restoration 73.6% to 82.5%.

These are the authors' figures on constructed abstractions of frozen traces. Appendix G states that live abstractions may differ and that restoration assumes the original provenance is still available.

Source: the same work, section 5.1 RQ3, section 5.2 and Appendix G, arxiv.org/abs/2611.18471v1.

Why a Knowledge Contract reader should care

A verifier verdict is an assessment of an execution made from the evidence available to the verifier; it is not by itself established knowledge. When a verdict crosses a compaction or delegation boundary and the evidence stays behind, the receiver holds a claim whose support it cannot inspect. That is a provenance problem, not only an accuracy problem. The paper measures how often a verifier stops producing a correct, usable judgment for the same execution when supporting evidence is hidden, and how often restoring that evidence recovers the judgment. It also shows that a lossy restoration recovers less than the exact source.

For reuse, this suggests two rules worth testing. A verdict reached on abstracted evidence should not be accepted on that basis alone. An ambiguous case should refuse or ask for the exact source rather than guess.

The paper's abstract names a public code repository (github.com/Disha1001/Verification-Transport). When we requested that address on 18 November 2026 at 04:39 UTC, it returned HTTP 404.

Source: the same work, abstract, sections 3.2 and 6, arxiv.org/abs/2611.18471v1.

What we proposed, and what has not happened

Our research desk assessed the paper on 17 November 2026 and proposed a trial, not adoption: take 20 approved frozen traces, one pinned verifier and the same ground truth; show each trace in three abstracted views and with the exact original evidence restored by hash; record verdict flips, refusals, missing provenance and cost. Acceptance would require that nothing is accepted on abstracted evidence alone and that every ambiguous case refuses or asks for the exact source.

The status is proposed. No owner has decided, nothing has run, and the specific Knowledge Contract clause it maps to is not yet identified.

Source of the definitions this trial would use (the trial itself is our proposal): the same work, section 3.1, arxiv.org/abs/2611.18471v1.

entry.title: Reasoning kept as code: API-based cost estimates and the break-even of reuse
entry.summary: Five researchers turned a large model's reasoning traces into small programs that execute as ordinary code on a CPU and call a small target model only for language operations. On eight benchmark sets the programs answered about as accurately as the source model and, on problems they already answered correctly, passed at least 90.8% of validated rewordings and re-parameterizations. Using March 2026 retail API rates, the authors estimate construction at the cost of 12 to 84 source calls and break-even at about 13 to 90 invocations of an applicable entry for similar questions; these figures do not measure the cost of a live request stream. We keep the work as a reference and have changed nothing.
entry.content:
Reusing a result is cheaper than producing it again only if the result is reused often enough and stays correct when the question changes a little. A study submitted on 6 November 2026 puts numbers on both conditions for one form of reuse: a language model's reasoning, rewritten as a program.

The method: a trace becomes a program

Peter Belcak, Greg Heinrich, Saurav Muralidharan, Shizhe Diao and Pavlo Molchanov start from the observation that language models solve every problem from scratch, although many solutions apply to a whole class of problems that differ in wording or in some parameters. Their method takes the transcript of a large source model solving one problem and has a builder model rewrite it in five phases: isolate input and expected output, decompose the reasoning into function-sized steps, recognise which parts of the input are parameters, plan the program, and implement it.

The result is a set of Python functions in which a small target model performs only the language operations. Each candidate function is tested against the corresponding fragment of the transcript. The finished entry is tested end to end against both the transcript and the benchmark's reference answer, and then with parameters extracted from the raw question by the small model. At serving time a new question is matched to an entry by embedding similarity; if nothing is similar enough, the question goes to the source model.

Source: Peter Belcak, Greg Heinrich, Saurav Muralidharan, Shizhe Diao, Pavlo Molchanov, "CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse", arXiv:2611.09891v1, 6 November 2026, arxiv.org/abs/2611.09891v1.

Accuracy against the reference and against the source

The evaluation covers six benchmarks in eight sets: competition and school mathematics, graduate science questions and a multidisciplinary set. Source and builder are the same large model; the target was first a small commercial model (Claude Haiku 4.5) and then a 1B-parameter model (Llama 3.2 1B) that the authors fine-tuned. The paper does not say which of the two produced each accuracy figure; the invocation cost is valued at rates for the 1B model.

Two quantities are reported per set. Cache accuracy is the share of benchmark problems for which the program gives the reference answer. Fidelity is the share for which judges find the program's answer equivalent to the source model's answer. Cache accuracy matched or exceeded source accuracy on seven of the eight sets, for example 93.3% against 83.3% on one mathematics set, and trailed on one, 98.0% against 98.5%. The authors attribute the gains to cases where the source reasons correctly and slips in the last steps, while the program executes the same reasoning as deterministic code. Fidelity exceeded 98% on six of eight sets.

One detail matters for reading these figures: construction checks each entry against the reference answer of the very problem it is later scored on.

Source: the same work, sections 2.2.1, 2.2.4 and 3.4 to 3.6, Table 2, arxiv.org/abs/2611.09891v1.

Does the program survive a changed question

Three tests vary the wording, the parameter values, or both. The pass rates are counted over rewritten problems that a committee of two judges accepted unanimously as faithful, and only for problems the program already answered correctly. Generator and judges are instances of the same model as the source. For changed parameters the expected answer is the generator's own worked solution, since the benchmark's reference no longer applies.

Under these conditions the programs handled at least 90% of rewritten problems in every set and mode; the lowest rate is 90.8%, for combined changes on one mathematics set. Combined changes gave the lowest rate in six of eight sets.

Source: the same work, sections 3.2, 3.4 and 3.6, arxiv.org/abs/2611.09891v1.

The price of reuse

The cost table reports API-based estimates per problem using March 2026 rates, in three figures: one source call, building the entry, one invocation of the program. An invocation costs $0.0004 to $0.0019, which is 16 to 291 times less than a source call. Building costs 12 to 84 source calls: lowest where the source reasons at length and the computation is simple, highest where the source answers briefly and the entry still needs full construction.

The authors give the break-even themselves: the build cost divided by the saving per call. An entry for the hardest mathematics problems pays for itself after approximately 13 invocations in its neighbourhood of similar questions, an entry for grade-school word problems after approximately 90. The cost of fine-tuning the small target model is not among the three figures. For that model the authors took 20% of the usage examples from the benchmark evaluations, had the source model produce a synthetic set about ten times larger, and fine-tuned on the resulting data; the cost of producing that set is also outside the three figures.

Source: the same work, sections 2.2.4, 3.1, 3.5 and 3.6, arxiv.org/abs/2611.09891v1.

What the study does not show

The benchmarks are mathematics and science questions with known answers. The authors say they chose them as a proxy for difficulty, not as the intended use, which is software where the same instructions meet varying payloads. The paper reports no rate of matches and fallbacks on a live stream of requests, and merging similar functions into a more general one is, in the authors' words, not addressed.

Source: the same work, sections 3.3 and 4, arxiv.org/abs/2611.09891v1.

What we take from it

We did not reproduce any of these numbers, and nothing in Knowledge Contract changed because of this study.

Knowledge Contract is about reusing knowledge within a stated scope and with evidence. This paper is useful to us as a worked example of the accounting. It separates three things that are easy to blur: fidelity to the source, agreement with a reference, and survival under a changed question. It also states the price of reuse as a break-even count, not as a ratio per call.

Our assessment keeps the paper as a reference and proposes one rule for our own reuse decisions: compute the break-even with the full fixed cost, including validation and training, and with the share of real requests that the reused artefact completes without falling back. A cheap call to an entry that already exists is not a cheap stream of tasks. The state is proposed; no owner has accepted it, and we are not building such a cache.

Source: Peter Belcak, Greg Heinrich, Saurav Muralidharan, Shizhe Diao, Pavlo Molchanov, "CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse", arXiv:2611.09891v1, arxiv.org/abs/2611.09891v1.

entry.title: Evidence cut along the execution record: in one study, source-aligned units delivered complete support more often than fixed token windows
entry.summary: Seven researchers asked when the recorded structure of an agent's execution helps its memory retrieve evidence. On 2,000 queries, units aligned to tool arguments and outputs put the complete evidence inside a 2,048-token budget 19.07 points more often than 512-token windows, and a graph step added 4.55 points more, primarily where evidence spans several events. We keep the result as a reference and have changed nothing.
entry.content:
A claim that rests on several pieces of evidence is supported only when all of them are in front of the reader. A study submitted on 22 September 2026 applies that standard to agent memory: under a hard token budget, does retrieval deliver every required piece, and does the recorded structure of the execution help?

The question and the measure

Yiqi Wang, Jinqian Ju, Jiaqi Zhang, Zequn Sun, Yiqun Duan, Mingkai Zheng and Taotao Cai treat retrieval from an agent's execution history as evidence completion. Each required item is an exact span in the original execution record, and every retrieved candidate maps back to the same source coordinates, so differently organised candidates can be scored against the same evidence.

Their main measure, Full Support, asks whether the retrieved candidates that fit the token budget cover every required span. The authors' reason: "partial evidence generally does not yield a correct answer."

The corpus, ISETrace, is synthetic: intents and interactions are generated, and the tool calls are executed in isolated operating-system environments. A language model wrote 2,000 queries over 1,207 held-out executions, each with one or more exact quotations from tool arguments or outputs; a quotation was accepted only if it located uniquely in its source event. The test set has 641 direct, 906 linked and 453 multi-fact queries.

Source: Yiqi Wang, Jinqian Ju, Jiaqi Zhang, Zequn Sun, Yiqun Duan, Mingkai Zheng, Taotao Cai, "When Does Execution Provenance Help Agent Memory Retrieval?", arXiv:2609.25913v1, 22 September 2026, arxiv.org/abs/2609.25913v1.

Units that follow the source beat fixed windows

The usual candidate is a fixed window of tokens. The authors build candidates from tool arguments and outputs instead, which they call provenance units. With the same fine-tuned dense scorer on both sides, provenance units raised Full Support at a 2,048-token budget by 19.07 points over 512-token windows. They stayed 11.96 points above an oracle that picks the best of four window sizes separately for each metric, a setting the authors call stronger than any single deployable one.

Shrinking the window does not rescue the flat view. Cutting it from 512 to 128 tokens raised Full Support at 2,048 tokens by 7.11 points, but the evidence was then scattered over more separately ranked candidates and early ranking fell.

The authors limit the claim themselves. The two views are not the same text cut differently: the flat view includes free-form messages and reasoning, while provenance units are restricted to tool arguments and outputs. They report the difference as an effect of the candidate view, "not a pure segmentation estimate".

Source: the same work, abstract and results on candidate views, arxiv.org/abs/2609.25913v1.

Graph gains concentrate where evidence spans several events

To isolate the graph, the authors hold the candidates and their dense scores fixed and add a learned correction over typed links between units. It adds 4.55 points of Full Support at 2,048 tokens, with a 95% interval of 2.98 to 6.18.

Split by query type, the gain is 0.19 points for direct queries, with an interval that includes zero, 4.00 for linked and 11.83 for multi-fact queries. Expanding flat chunks through an entity co-occurrence graph, by contrast, never differed from keyword retrieval by more than 1.1 points on any budgeted metric in their main table.

The hard case stays hard. On multi-fact queries the graph variant reaches 62.25 on Full Support at 2,048 tokens, so, in the authors' words, "more than one third of multi-fact queries still lack complete support".

Source: the same work, results on the graph-conditioned residual, arxiv.org/abs/2609.25913v1.

Does complete evidence give better answers

On a prespecified group of 315 linked and multi-fact queries, a judge that never saw the method scored strict answer accuracy at 71.75% with flat windows, 75.56% with provenance units and 77.78% with the graph variant. With the exact evidence supplied the figure is 86.35%; with no evidence, 1.27%.

The difference between the graph variant and flat windows is 6.03 points with a 95% interval of 0.00 to 12.10. The authors call this "borderline evidence" and describe the link between support and accuracy as "mechanistic consistency rather than causal identification".

Source: the same work, downstream answer study, arxiv.org/abs/2609.25913v1.

Limits the authors state

The queries were written by a language model from selected source packets. A human validator reviewed model judgments on 500 of them and did not re-annotate them blind; after correction, gold evidence is accurate for 96.0% and complete for 96.2%, and the human query type agrees with the authored one for 77.8%, so the three type labels are noisy. The graph is compiled from observable call and return structure, and the authors say a link in it "does not demonstrate semantic causality". They do not present the dataset as a community benchmark until a reviewed release is frozen, and they warn that exact-history retrieval can expose sensitive material without access control and redaction.

Source: the same work, limitations and ethical considerations, arxiv.org/abs/2609.25913v1.

What we take from it

We did not reproduce any of these numbers, and nothing in Knowledge Contract changed because of this study.

Two points are relevant to our work on reusing knowledge with its source kept. First, the measure: counting whether all required evidence arrived, not whether some relevant fragment did, matches how a bound claim has to be checked. Second, the order of effects: the shape of the evidence unit mattered several times more than the graph step, and in this evaluation the measured gains of the graph were concentrated on evidence spread over several events.

Our assessment keeps the paper as a reference and proposes one bounded trial: on 40 to 100 preselected synthetic traces, compare source-aligned evidence units with fixed windows under the same corpus, the same access and the same 2,048-token cap, and score exact-span completeness and independently checked answer accuracy. A graph runtime stays on hold until a cost-matched baseline supports it. The state is proposed; no owner has accepted it.

Source: Yiqi Wang, Jinqian Ju, Jiaqi Zhang, Zequn Sun, Yiqun Duan, Mingkai Zheng, Taotao Cai, "When Does Execution Provenance Help Agent Memory Retrieval?", arXiv:2609.25913v1, arxiv.org/abs/2609.25913v1.

entry.title: Tech diplomacy: making an agent's knowledge, authority and results inspectable
entry.summary: Following Yurii Chudinov's recommendation, we read the primary files of GPT Deprivation and Tech Diplomacy, correct our DORA summary and propose a bounded Knowledge Contract experiment. The research proposals, our laboratory design and possible cooperation with TDGI have different evidence and different next steps.
entry.content:
An agent can cite the right document and still use it outside its scope. It can finish a task and still lack permission for one of the actions it took. It can describe a successful result that another participant cannot verify. These are distinct problems, and an explanation of agent reliability needs to show how they connect.

On 16 November, Yurii Chudinov recommended a closer reading of two works associated with Albina Dermenzhy and clarified our account of the DORA study. We opened the primary files. This article explains what the works establish, what they propose and what we want to test with Knowledge Contract. It also introduces a separate institutional direction: possible dialogue with the Paris-based Tech Diplomacy Global Institute (TDGI).

DORA: apply the existing framework and account for the gaps

Our 14 November article now carries a dated correction. Its earlier statement about ICT resilience came from section 1 of the original work. The summary did not adequately convey the practical conclusion in sections 14–15: use existing DORA mechanisms for AI services within the Regulation's scope, while addressing the identified gaps in criteria, controls and evidence. Chudinov's clarification is that this application does not first require amendments to the provisions.

The authors propose four connected layers: the DORA core, AI/model controls, other applicable requirements, and a common evidence trail. Inventory, change management, incident handling, testing and supplier management remain the operating processes. Their 35 gaps are an analytical result; identifying one does not automatically establish a violation, and their proposed controls do not certify a service. DORA has applied since 17 January 2025; that is its application date, not its entry-into-force date.

Source: Yurii Chudinov, Volodymyr Tkach, Albina Dermenzhy, Dmytro Aksenov and Serhii Vatylyk, Resilient Systems, Unverified Decisions: A Layer-by-Layer Projection of DORA onto AI Services in the EU Financial Sector, 1 November 2026, sections 3.2 and 14–15, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23857406; Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, Article 64.

GPT Deprivation: the boundary of trust is task-specific

GPT Deprivation investigates how expectations about an AI system can exceed its capabilities in a particular task. One proposed mechanism is the transfer of trust earned on familiar work to a domain where the user lacks the expertise needed to evaluate the answer. The practical recommendation is to define the assignment and limits of trust before work, then verify the output before a consequential irreversible action.

Its evidence needs careful reading. The work combines several distinct corpora, including a sample of 30 court cases and a separate set of 33 lawsuits against vendors. Those are not one independent sample and should not be added together. The lawsuits describe allegations; the paper does not establish all alleged events or causation through judgments on the merits.

Section 5.9 shows how the trust-transfer conclusion depends on the coding rule. The following figures refer to the same 33-lawsuit corpus, not to all AI users:

Coding condition Transfer among cases with known values Unknown cases out of 33 Reported conclusion
Evaluation of the new task is not described 21 of 22 11 Supported under this rule
The document explicitly states that no verification occurred 9 of 10 23 Not established under the study's threshold
Isolation from people able to check also qualifies 18 of 19 14 Supported under this rule

This does not estimate how often AI causes harm, or measure how much a mandate reduces it. The study was assembled around documented adverse cases. A test of protective measures also needs intercepted errors, false stops and successful ordinary use. For our laboratory, the useful hypothesis is narrower: task-specific applicability checks may prevent inappropriate reuse, and that effect must be measured against a stated comparator.

Source: GPT Deprivation: How the Wrong Point on the Ontology and Expectations Scale Leads to Losses from Generative AI. A Multiple-Case Study, 2023–2026, published in Albina Dermenzhy's Zenodo record, v1, 23 October 2026, sections 3, 5.9, 7–8, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23599162. The record credits Dermenzhy as Editor. We read pages 1–12, 22–34 and 44–49, with relevant codebook and deviation-log sections; we did not independently recode the cases.

Tech Diplomacy: a proposal for continuing coordination

Albina Dermenzhy's Tech Diplomacy extends the term to interaction between people, probabilistic systems and other systems. Its eight functions cover a shared interaction frame, translation into technical criteria, delegation of authority, shared state and evidence, challenge and escalation, continuing assurance, supplier coordination, and remediation and learning. The framework asks participants to revise their working arrangements when the system, context or consequences change.

The appendices describe nine linked objects, including an Interaction Charter, AI Mandate, Acceptance Profile and Evidence Graph. They favour a connected data model with views for different roles, rather than nine disconnected documents. That is a useful question for an engineering team: can the decision, its authority and its evidence still be followed after a handoff?

The proposal's limits are explicit. It has not been tested through deployments; the sufficiency of a mandate is untested. Treating trust as a current state is a normative position. The metrics appendix leaves calculation methods, data sources and thresholds to later work. Its financial scenario is illustrative. We therefore treat the framework as a source of hypotheses and design requirements to evaluate.

Source: Albina Dermenzhy, Tech Diplomacy: A Framework for Interaction Between Probabilistic Systems, Humans, and Other Systems, v1, 12 November 2026, sections 4, 6–7 and appendices A, D–I, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24172092. We read the 20-page explanatory note and 11-page appendices. The PDF names Dermenzhy as author; Zenodo classifies the record as a Proposal.

A proposed mapping to Knowledge Contract

The mapping below is ours. It is not an assertion that the frameworks have identical schemas or that the integration is already implemented. We will first reuse existing entities and owners; a new term alone is not a reason to create another registry.

Question raised by the framework What our experiment must make inspectable
What was agreed for this interaction? The task, applicable knowledge, constraints and acceptance criteria, with exact versions.
Who may act, and within which limits? A current authorization for the action, checked separately from the relevance of a knowledge artifact.
What did the agent actually use? The source passage, artifact revision and content received at the actual computation boundary. Retrieval alone is insufficient.
What happened, and can it be challenged? An execution record, result check and a route to stop or contest the action, independent of the agent's final narrative.
What changed after a failure? The affected result and reuse links, a reproducible counterexample, a reviewed successor and a later checked application.

A valid document hash proves identity of bytes. It does not grant access, establish semantic fit, prove that those bytes were used or accept the resulting work. Likewise, changing a model's name does not by itself establish independent verification. The trial must record the relevant controller, evidence and review procedure.

Source: our proposed crosswalk from Dermenzhy's sections 6–7 and appendices A–B to the Knowledge Contract core specification and API integration appendix. This is a design proposal, not a new permission or measured implementation result.

One source, two tasks and a visible reason for every transition

We propose a small experiment with a source whose use is permitted. A passage supplies a rule and its conditions. Task one asks an agent to check a proposed knowledge-package update against that rule. The display should show the selected passage, extracted candidate, review and admission, the resolver's choice, the tool's actual input, the result and its separate acceptance. Missing evidence must remain visible.

Task two checks a distinct knowledge-package update and reuses the accepted artifact. Between controlled runs, we change the source version, revoke an action permission or make a premise incompatible. The expected response is determined in advance: retrieve the new eligible version, refuse an unauthorized effect or replan the affected step. An obsolete artifact must not silently retain its former applicability. A harmless wording change is a separate control, so mere change detection cannot masquerade as understanding.

We will record two outcomes separately: did an unauthorized action occur, and did the intended task meet its acceptance criteria? A refusal may prevent an unsafe effect while leaving the task incomplete. A breakdown is another result. The comparison needs the same tasks, budgets and evidence rules, with unknown values retained. Time, total cost, intercepted mistakes, false stops and successful reuse belong in the result, not just a count of completed runs.

This describes the next test we intend to perform. It does not report a completed protected run or prove that every stage of Live Lab works. Its value will come from the actual evidence that a reader can inspect on both sites.

Source: our experimental proposal, informed by GPT Deprivation, sections 7–8, and Tech Diplomacy, appendix H; Knowledge Contract API integration.

TDGI: a possible institutional conversation

TDGI's institutional work concerns technology, international relations and governance. Its AI Diplomacy Council addresses cooperation with, about and through AI. That scope differs from Dermenzhy's framework for individual and organizational interaction. Connecting them through an inspectable agent case is our proposal; shared terminology does not establish an institutional relationship.

We are preparing a capability brief and a possible workshop on evidence, agent mandates and reusable knowledge. The Institute's free community offers an initial route to learn about its work. Its Global Assembly is announced for 11 December 2026 in Paris; attendance requires confirmation by its Secretariat. Any contribution to an event or joint programme would need separate agreement. Neither Arcanada nor Knowledge Contract claims TDGI membership, Fellowship, partnership or endorsement in this article.

The further project route worth assessing is Global 5X AI. Its stated requirement is an execution-ready project with measurable public benefit over 100 days, a responsible owner, authority, resources and an operating environment. We would consider that route after a real bounded laboratory result and a suitable beneficiary are established. The Assembly is an opportunity for dialogue; it is not a prerequisite for our engineering work.

Source: TDGI's AI Diplomacy Council, Community, Global Assembly and Global 5X AI pages, checked 16 November 2026. The cooperation and workshop described here are our plans.

entry.title: A rule after restart: from a repository snapshot to a local calculation
entry.summary: A new offline consumer connects the repository session to Source Rule Checks. Before each new evaluation request it observes the committed inputs again; changed context requires an explicit resume. The candidate prepares a laboratory workflow without connecting the public lab or calling a language model.
entry.content:
A program can calculate a rule correctly and still use the wrong revision of it. After a pause, a source file may have changed while the agent remembers its earlier reading. The next engineering step in Knowledge Contract addresses that boundary: which exact source and interpretation packet may a local calculation use now?

The cited revision is the candidate in open PR 119; the observations below come from local execution.

One calculation, one observed context

The candidate joins two existing components: the repository session, which records and adopts a bounded context, and Semantic Bridge, which evaluates explicitly supplied rules and alternative readings. Its complete file profile contains two committed inputs: the rule source and its interpretation packet. Both are required.

Starting a ready session adopts a context; it does not yet evaluate the rule. Each new "EVALUATE" request first makes a fresh repository observation. If the adopted context is no longer usable, the calculation is blocked. An explicit resume can adopt the newly observed context, after which a new evaluation checks it again. The bridge receives the exact bytes retained in that observation, rather than reopening the working-tree files after the check.

Source: the candidate implementation, repository_rule_consumer.py, and the source change.

What the local run actually checked

The completed local run matched the predeclared outcome at all 12 steps: 11 fresh consumer captures and one historical inspection. This was one authored sequence in a real local Git repository, not 12 independent trials. An unknown rule outcome remained undetermined; changing the interpretation packet blocked evaluation until an explicit resume; an unrelated commit preserved the accepted context. After an unsupported rule source was adopted, the bridge returned "UNSUPPORTED", with no truth result. Uncommitted decoy edits did not replace the captured committed inputs.

The first run stopped at step two because its authored example packet lacked required observation fields. The program refused that input. The example was corrected, and the failed run was retained alongside the completed run; it was not replaced by a success report.

A separate input review found that the capture-count limit was checked only after replaying the supplied history. The correction moves that guard before hashing and replay. Its synthetic boundary controls check early refusal of an oversized history; they are separate from the twelve-step lifecycle.

The retained result binds the input identities, repository observation, adopted context and calculation in one receipt. Inspecting a saved receipt recomputes the recorded result from its retained bytes, without making a new Git observation. It checks internal consistency and reports a historical result; it does not claim that the repository still has those contents.

Source: the actual lifecycle receipt and the non-author review.

What this does not settle

The observation covers committed files at the recorded capture. It does not cover arbitrary uncommitted edits, the meaning of unrestricted prose, every dependency of a real task or changes after the capture. The receipt chain is not an authenticated signature or a guarantee of complete history. A successful calculation grants no permission to act.

The controlled rule grammar, manual interpretation packet and unknown observations keep their existing boundaries. No language-model call is needed for this local workflow. Review carried out by another task on the same controller, model family and host is internal non-author review, not external independence.

Source: the consumer's declared scope and the Semantic Bridge specification.

A preparation step for the laboratory

This is an offline engineering step. The public Knowledge Journey page still reports that it is unconnected, with upload and start controls disabled. Its existing observation and retained-file components are delivered as assets; that alone does not connect a producer, establish access to a private object or start a run.

The next laboratory integration can consume the same bounded receipts and distinguish an observed calculation from a historical one. A live browser connection still needs its own source binding, permitted read path, session lifecycle and actual browser acceptance. This journal entry records source work; it does not advance the published corpus pin or announce a production connection.

Source: Knowledge Journey, its existing reader boundary and the asset readback of 15 November 2026.

entry.title: Source rule checks: a supplied rule, its exception and two readings carried through a checkable computation
entry.summary: A new engineering study in the Knowledge Contract corpus asks whether a bounded program can keep a stated rule, its exception, alternative readings and unknown facts intact while computing with them. Against a separately written oracle it matched on 16,384 and 4,096 finite cases, and a review by a non-author found one real input failure, now fixed. It is a finite check, not language understanding.
entry.content:
A rule in a source often comes with an exception, and a reader may hold two readings of it. A program that computes with the rule can lose either one quietly: by clipping the exception, by merging the readings, or by treating an unknown fact as false. A study merged into the Knowledge Contract corpus on 15 November 2026 tests whether a small, bounded program keeps all three.

The question and the answer

The study, "Source Rule Checks: Finite Binding, Alternatives and Operation Composition", asks: "Can a bounded consumer preserve an explicitly supplied rule, its exception, alternative readings and unknown observations through a checkable computation?" Its input is a short authored source with NOTE and RULE lines and a supplied interpretation packet. It is explicitly "not an automatic extractor of meaning from unrestricted prose".

Each rule line must match its byte selector, its quoted text and the source digest, so a clipped prefix that drops "UNLESS suspended" is refused even when the hash of the source is valid. Unknown and withheld values both allow false and true but stay distinguishable. Every report keeps source fidelity, attribution, real-world truth and current authority as not assessed, and states that no effects are authorized.

Source: Pavel Valentov, "Source Rule Checks: Finite Binding, Alternatives and Operation Composition", Knowledge Contract engineering study, edition 1.1, github.com/Arcanada-one/knowledge-contract.

Against an oracle written separately

The expected results come from a suite that starts from Boolean truth masks and does not use the implementation's tokenizer, parser or evaluator. The study is direct about what this separation is: the oracle "was authored by a separate task from the implementation" but "shares the controller, model family and host", so it is "not external independence".

The program matched that oracle on two complete finite families:

  • all 256 Boolean functions of three variables under 64 availability profiles: 16,384 records, of which 2,952 true, 2,952 false and 10,480 undetermined;
  • all 256 ordered pairs of two-variable functions under 16 profiles: 4,096 records, with 1,088 agreements and 3,008 same-world disagreements between the two readings.

In 984 of those pair records, the two readings have the same set of possible values and still disagree in the same world. A check that compares only the sets would call them equal. The counters are checked against the declared complete inventories, so a missing function or profile cannot pass with a smaller denominator.

Source: the same study, sections "Independent expected-result method" and the finite receipt, github.com/Arcanada-one/knowledge-contract.

Where it meets the existing algebra

Four integration tests feed the program's output into the corpus's existing relation and outcome-set geometry code. One shows why aggregate distances are not enough. Two eligibility readings have the same outcome set, Hausdorff distance zero, and still disagree in two of eight common worlds. The study reads this as consistent with the stated scope of two earlier papers in the corpus, not as a counterexample to them. Another test shows that a row index of zero can carry the meaning "true", so row numbers cannot stand in for Boolean labels.

Source: the same study, section "Connection to algebra and geometry", github.com/Arcanada-one/knowledge-contract.

A failure that was kept

A review by a non-author sent a 5,341-byte packet containing a 5,000-digit integer in a byte selector. The packet was under the size limit, and the first implementation crashed with a Python traceback and no JSON result. The corrected reader turns such decoder errors into a structured refusal: exit 2, INVALID, malformed_json, nothing evaluated. The original module, the failed output and the corrected output are kept side by side, "the first failure was not overwritten by success". The reviewer then ran 30 further probes and found no remaining blocker within that scope, which the study states is not an exhaustive proof.

Source: the same study, section "Resolved input failure and review boundary", github.com/Arcanada-one/knowledge-contract.

Our state

Integrated: the study, its specification ("Semantic Bridge: From Source Readings to Checkable Operations", an engineering draft) and the code are on the main branch of the public Knowledge Contract repository since 15 November 2026. The review recorded for them is a review by a non-author on the same model family, not independent review.

Open, in the study's own words: general human-to-formal fidelity, quantifiers, units, time, nested attribution, required media, complete artifact integration and actual agent use. Publication decisions, index admission and native admission have separate criteria. No paid experiment was run.

Source: Knowledge Contract, merged pull request 118, github.com/Arcanada-one/knowledge-contract/pull/118.

entry.title: Agent Situation: keeping a bounded view current
entry.summary: A new research draft examines how an agent establishes its situation, responds to change and selects context for a task. The programme separates finite controls, a planned language-model trial and eventual runtime use.
entry.content:
An agent returns to a conversation with a detailed account of yesterday's work. The active account, repository revision or outcome of a pending operation may already have changed. How should it establish what is current, what remains uncertain and what matters to its next step?

Agent Situation: Initialization, Change, and Bounded Context develops this question as a research draft within Knowledge Contract's existing Agent Application programme. This article is an editorial introduction; scientific acceptance and full-text translation review remain separate work.

Begin with a partial situation

The draft proposes an initial inventory of the task, operating scope, relevant participants, available tools, ongoing operations, constraints, uncertainties and resources. Each operation selects the fields it needs. Repository maintenance may require a branch revision and build status; a physical agent may require a local reference frame and sensor observations.

Missing information stays explicit. A saved description does not establish today's account or permissions. Initialization has a bounded deadline and can support a limited response while leaving other operations unresolved. Source: research draft and engineering design.

Follow relevant changes

The proposed lifecycle connects observations to the conclusions and plans that depend on them. A changed prerequisite invalidates the affected view. A later message can contain older information, and receiving an observation again does not make it newer.

Acquisition, state updates, context selection and model calls have separate schedules. Relevant events can trigger a focused update; expiry rules provide a backstop. Conflicting observations retain their sources and scope. An uncertain external outcome calls for reconciliation before a repeated action. Source: change and refresh proposal.

Preserve the conditions needed for a decision

A model receives a selected view under a resource budget. The proposal retains declared mandatory dependencies, relevant uncertainty and an account of omissions. If required material cannot fit, the system exposes that limit and considers a smaller task or another representation.

This extends the existing Context Package vocabulary. Including a condition still leaves a further question: did the agent use it correctly? Source: bounded-context argument.

Test the proposal in separate stages

The reading record now covers 21 selected primary sources across situation awareness, context-aware systems, robotics and agent memory. Two close architectural predecessors have been added: CoALA describes persistent working memory and selected inputs for each model call; CoDRA separates context observers from robot execution. The review remains targeted. Recent preprints retain their status; Scroll contributes an abstract-level comparison, and mutable ROS documentation has recorded access dates.

The companion Context Controls study reports 21 of 21 authored finite checks passing, with all three selected disabled-guard variants detected. The initial 18 checks missed a delayed-derivation defect; review exposed it, and the correction added three controls. These are local state-model checks, with no LLM calls or real authorization mechanism. The review used agents under the same controller; external independence is not established.

A continuation review found a separate defect in the test runner: omitting one registered check let it execute only 20 of the 21 expected cases and still report success. The repair passed nine separate checks of registration completeness and result accounting. These nine checks have their own scope and count, alongside the 21 model checks and three disabled-guard variants. The state model and literal expected outcomes are unchanged, and the historical evidence is preserved.

A separate, unexecuted LLM protocol proposes comparison with a strong deterministic state manager under matched resources, measuring valid task completion, stale-value use, unnecessary refusal and total cost. Conditions 4 and 5 share the same frozen projector, optional ranking, guards and budgets; only the optional acquisition and refresh schedule changes. This comparison is designed to isolate selective refresh, while a separate benefit from projection would need its own comparison. The allocation remains 450 proposed episode-runs; none of those LLM runs have been executed. No performance gain or cost saving is reported.

Further review and a bounded pilot remain planned. The results may support a simpler deterministic design. Source: literature, finite-study scope and experiment plan.

entry.title: Thirty-five gaps: a legal analysis maps DORA onto AI services, and three of them concern agents
entry.summary: Five authors project the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act onto AI services in finance and record 35 places where, in their reading, the rules give no criterion. Three concern agents: review by an agent in the same environment, an agent's own report, and an agent testing the system it runs. It is the authors' analysis, not a measurement, and we read only part of it.
entry.content:
Editorial correction, 16 November 2026. Following Yurii Chudinov’s clarification, we have revised the summary below. The statement about DORA and ICT resilience did appear in section 1 of the source; our summary did not convey the conclusion in sections 14–15: apply the existing framework to AI while accounting for the identified gaps. We have also corrected the date-of-application wording and narrowed the AI Act classification claim. The original publication date is retained.

What does a resilience law written for IT systems say when the system is an AI service? A work published on 1 November 2026 answers for one law, the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554), and one sector, finance. Its answer is a list of 35 gaps, each derived by the same five steps. For the original review published on 14 November, we read the summary, the method, the closing sections and three of the gap chains. At that point we had not checked its quotations of the law against the official texts. The additional reading and limited legal checks for this correction are described below.

What the work claims

The authors examine how existing DORA requirements can be applied to AI services used by financial entities within the Regulation’s scope, without amending its provisions. Their method maps the requirements to the components of an AI service and accounts for the identified gaps when choosing criteria, controls and evidence. Chudinov’s clarification of 16 November makes the central point explicit: apply DORA to AI while accounting for these gaps, rather than amend the Regulation first.

Sections 14–15 propose four connected layers: the existing DORA framework, AI-specific controls, other regulatory requirements where applicable, and a single evidence trail. The AI controls are embedded in existing inventory, change management, incident handling, testing and supplier processes. This is the authors’ proposed way to address the gaps; the list does not, by itself, establish compliance or correct AI decisions. DORA has applied since 17 January 2025. Article 64 distinguishes that date from its entry into force.

The object they analyse is not the model. It is the AI service: the model together with what surrounds it in operation, such as data, prompts and guardrails, retrieval, the agent layer, providers, human oversight and fallback.

Across eight layers of DORA they record 35 gaps: 2 in governance, 6 in inventory and change, 4 in detection and continuity, 5 in incidents, 10 in testing, 5 in providers, 2 in oversight and 1 in information sharing. The counts are ours, taken from the table in section 2.3.

In sections 13.4–13.5, the authors compare DORA with the EU AI Act, including creditworthiness assessment and life and health insurance. They interpret the rules for financial entities as connecting monitoring with governance under financial law and, through it, DORA. This is their reading of the relationship between the frameworks, not an exhaustive classification. Article 6 and Annex III of the AI Act require a system-specific assessment: recruitment and workers’ management are also listed uses, including when such systems are used by a financial organisation. Calling a system a chatbot, an internal assistant or a development agent does not, by itself, establish that its intended use is outside the high-risk categories.

Source: Yurii Chudinov, Volodymyr Tkach, Albina Dermenzhy, Dmytro Aksenov, Serhii Vatylyk, "Resilient Systems, Unverified Decisions: A Layer-by-Layer Projection of DORA onto AI Services in the EU Financial Sector", Zenodo, 1 November 2026, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23857406. For the regulatory scope, definitions and application date: DORA, Articles 1–3 and 64. For classification: AI Act, Article 6 and Annex III.

How a gap is derived

A gap is recorded only when five steps hold. One: DORA or its technical standards contain a norm that applies, shown by a verbatim quotation. Two: the norm is projected onto a specific element of the AI service. Three: a property of AI creates a failure mode the norm does not account for. Four: the norm gives no criterion, threshold or evidence for that case. Five: the consequence needs another layer of control.

The work says which steps are whose. Step one rests on a quotation. Steps two and five are marked "author's projection". If a step fails, no gap is recorded. Its example: prompt injection is specific to AI, but a data leak through it already meets the definition of an ICT-related incident, so step four fails and there is no gap.

It also limits what the word means: a gap "does not mean an automatic violation of DORA, nor does it mean an absence of regulation altogether".

This is the part closest to our subject: every conclusion says what kind of support it has, so a quoted norm and the authors' reading of it can be told apart.

Source: the same work, section 3.2, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23857406.

Three gaps about agents

We read three chains in full.

G-30. DORA's standards require that whoever approves a change is independent of whoever requests and implements it. The authors argue that changes made by AI outgrow what a person can read, so review passes to another AI, often in the same environment with shared context. The norm does not say whether such a reviewer is independent. Their remedy is to separate the reviewer's context, credentials and resources from the executor's, and to check the reviewer's conclusions against an action log.

G-31. DORA requires mechanisms to detect anomalous activity. The norm does not separate an executor's own report from evidence of its actions. For an agent, the authors write, the final answer is model output like any other and "may be incomplete or false". Detection should rely on action logs that the agent cannot modify.

G-35. DORA requires tests by independent parties. The norm is written for people and organisations and does not say whether an agent that operates a system is a party to testing it. The authors' consequence: such an agent is not admitted to testing that system.

We did not open the incident registry that the chains cite.

Source: the same work, sections 5.6, 6.6 and 8.6, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23857406.

What this changes for us, and what waits

At the original publication on 14 November, we had made no engineering changes because of this work. For that article we checked our own review records of 13 and 14 November, not every record we keep. In those records, a review of one agent's work by another agent is written as "a review by a non-author", and its independence is marked as not verified. In the same records, claims about a change are checked against the change itself, not against a report about it.

One thing those records do not establish is independence. The agents described there worked under one account and with models of one family. As recorded on 14 November, separation of their context, credentials and resources in the sense G-30 uses had not been verified, and no task for it had been identified. The recorded state was on hold; this editorial correction does not establish a new engineering result.

Limits. This is a legal analysis by its authors, published on Zenodo; we saw no sign of peer review in the parts we read. It is not a measurement and not a regulator’s position. The original review covered sections 1, 2, 3, 12 to 15 and the three chains. On 16 November we returned to the original Markdown, checked sections 1–2, 3.2 and 13.4–15, and read findings F-02 through F-07 in the findings registry. That registry labels F-02 as a projection of a norm, F-03 as a finding from projection and F-05 as a conceptual proposal. The other 32 chains and the incident sources remain unchecked. For the correction, we checked relevant official EUR-Lex passages on DORA’s scope, definitions and application date and on AI Act classification; we did not audit every legal quotation or every file in the research record.

Source: the same work, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23857406.

Further reading: update of 16 November

At the original publication on 14 November, we had seen only the metadata for the following two records and had opened none of their files. On 16 November we opened the primary PDFs. For GPT Deprivation we read the methods, findings and limitations; for Tech Diplomacy we read the full explanatory note and its appendices.

The Zenodo record for "GPT Deprivation: How the Wrong Point on the Ontology and Expectations Scale Leads to Losses from Generative AI. A Multiple-Case Study, 2023–2026" credits Albina Dermenzhy as editor. The work examines how trust earned on familiar tasks can carry over to a new domain without the corresponding competence or verification. It reconstructs publicly documented incidents and lawsuits; this is not an experiment or an estimate of how often harm occurs among users. Its practical proposal is to bound trust for the particular task and verify an output before a consequential irreversible action. The effectiveness of those safeguards is not measured by this corpus. Source: sections 3, 5.9, 7 and 8, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23599162.

Albina Dermenzhy’s "Tech Diplomacy: A Framework for Interaction Between Probabilistic Systems, Humans, and Other Systems" proposes ongoing coordination between people and AI services: clarify intent, turn it into criteria, bound authority, preserve state and evidence, challenge or escalate a result, check behaviour, coordinate suppliers and remedy consequences. Section 4 retains the four-layer DORA composition. Section 7 explicitly says the framework has not been tested through deployments; it is a proposal, not demonstrated effectiveness. Source: sections 4, 6 and 7, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24172092. Our follow-up on tech diplomacy and knowledge contracts separates the authors’ claims from the hypotheses we plan to test.

An article by Chuck Brooks of 24 October 2026 names the first author of the DORA work as co-founder of Compilence, which plans a hospital programme in Japan. In the metadata, descriptions and file names checked for the original 14 November review, none of the three records above mentioned that programme. That historical check did not establish that the research had been deployed in a hospital. bizcatalyst360.com.

entry.title: A research agent's verdict is not a test of known size
entry.summary: A study plants the truth in simulated data and scores what language-model research agents conclude. In simulated worlds with nothing to find, built without the repeated-value flaw of the earlier runs, three commercial research agents still claimed a finding in 34%, 16% and 44% of cases. A sentence about earlier research also changed verdicts on identical data.
entry.content:
When an agent analyses data and reports that it found something, who decided that the finding is real? Usually the agent itself. A new study measures how often that decision is wrong when the right answer is known in advance. We have not reproduced it. Below is what it shows and why it matters for any rule about reusing a result.

The truth is planted, so every verdict can be scored

Chang Liu gives each agent a simulated world whose data-generating process the author controls. Most worlds are monthly return series in which one of eight candidate predictors carries a planted signal of chosen strength, or none at all; the other seven are distractors with no predictive power. The agent sees 700 months, writes and runs its own code within a budget of 40 calls, and submits a model with a verdict: the model beats a static benchmark, does not beat it, or the search is abandoned. A further 360 months never enter the agent's sandbox and are used only to evaluate what it submitted.

Because the truth is known by construction, the agent can be treated like any statistical test. Two quantities matter. Size is how often it claims a finding in a world without a signal. Power is how often it detects a signal that is there. The author scores the verdict against the conventional 5% level, although the brief names no level: which threshold the agent applies on its own is one of the things measured.

Source: Chang Liu, "Are LLM Research Agents Reliable Judges of Predictability? Evidence from Planted-Signal Worlds", arXiv:2611.04070v1.

A finding was reported where there was nothing to find

In the first two studies, three commercial models claimed predictability in 21%, 19% and 63% of the worlds without a signal. An external review then found a flaw in the worlds: resampled shock values repeated exactly, so a lookup of past returns could forecast even an empty world, and the model with the highest rate exploited it. A third study replaced those shocks with Gaussian ones. The rates became 34%, 16% and 44%, and each model still claimed more often than a conventional test run on the same worlds. An open-weight model that runs on one workstation claimed in 35% of the empty worlds, and its rate barely rose when a signal was planted.

The agent of the first study did detect weak signals more often than a conventional out-of-sample test. The author's explanation is that it accepts weaker evidence. Held to the same false-positive rate, a conventional in-sample test with a correction for multiple candidates detected weak signals about as often, and more often than the model with the highest false-claim rate.

The stated confidence added little. In all 3,990 runs of the three commercial models, the agent claimed a finding exactly when its stated probability was at least one half. In the author's words, the implicit rule is a 50% posterior, not a 5% test.

Source: Chang Liu, the same paper, sections 1, 4 to 5 and 7.1, arXiv:2611.04070v1.

One sentence about prior research moved the verdict

In the first study, 160 worlds were run three times with the same data and one sentence changed at the end of the brief: nothing, a remark that prior research found a signal, or a remark that it found none. The share of worlds in which the agent claimed a finding was 32% under the sceptical sentence, 46% under the neutral brief and 61% under the optimistic one. The verdict differed between framings in 50 of the 160 worlds. In the worlds without a signal, the optimistic sentence raised false claims from 15% to 32%. In the worlds with a signal, the sceptical sentence lowered detection from 56% to 40%.

Source: Chang Liu, the same paper, section 3.3, arXiv:2611.04070v1.

What the author recommends, and where the evidence stops

The protocol the paper proposes is short: give a neutral brief; let the agent build the model but not issue the verdict; fix the decision rule in advance, outside the agent; keep the holdout technically out of its reach. The author says plainly that the last item is enforced by his harness and was not tested as a factor.

A sealed holdout is not free. In an exploratory analysis of the models the agents submitted in the third study, a holdout test at the 5% level claimed in at most 5% of the empty worlds, but for the three commercial models it detected only 25% to 28% of the worlds whose planted signal explains 1% of the variance, against 54% for the in-sample test. The author therefore treats the holdout as confirmation and an efficient pre-specified test as the primary rule.

The limits are stated in the paper. One agent configuration, one tool set and one brief were studied. The worlds are stylised: one planted predictor among eight. The false-positive rate that anchors the matched comparisons rests on 40 worlds. Two of the models were served under names without dated snapshots. The pre-specifications were recorded in repository commits, not in a public registry, and several of the stronger comparisons were designed after the first results were known.
